metadata.title: A critical review and meta-analysis of studies investigating the effects of the professional development teachers typically receive

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This publication is a systematic review and meta-analysis of existing studies rather than an analysis of a single ILSA micro-dataset. Consequently, it does not apply a unified set of student sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures to a pooled student-level sample. Instead, the review codes whether included primary studies reported probability weights, clustering/nesting adjustments, and plausible values handling, noting that less than half of the studies provided sufficient information about sampling weights and that many did not adjust for clustering/nesting. For interpreting the meta-analytic results, the key implication is that primary-study weighting and PV practices vary substantially, which can affect the precision of estimated associations and the credibility of standard errors across studies.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a systematic review/meta-analysis that synthesizes effect sizes reported in primary studies rather than estimating student-level outcomes from ILSA plausible values. Plausible values handling is therefore not applicable at the level of this review’s own analysis. Missing-data handling is not reported because the review does not perform a single imputation/deletion procedure on a unified dataset; instead, it describes that some primary studies lacked sufficient information for effect-size calculation and were excluded from the meta-analysis.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The review includes peer-reviewed and other English-language studies that (1) examine effects of Grades 1–12 teachers’ professional development (PD) participation on outcomes (not merely PD participation, perceptions, or informal learning), (2) focus on PD participation in general rather than effects of a specific PD program, and (3) use samples representative at national or state level. The authors searched ERIC, Scopus, and Web of Science (Nov 2024), supplemented with hand-searches and reference-list screening, and selected 68 papers in total. For the meta-analysis, they further restricted to outcome variables with enough effect-size information: student achievement and teachers’ self-reported teaching/instructional practices; studies lacking sufficient information for effect-size computation were excluded (some authors were contacted but did not provide enough data).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This article is a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the effects of teachers’ typical professional development (PD) participation using nationally or state-representative datasets. It synthesizes 68 included studies and conducts meta-analyses for two outcome families: student achievement and teachers’ instructional practices/teaching practices, using Pearson’s r as the effect-size metric (converted to Fisher’s z and back to correlations) and robust variance estimation with a random-effects model. Across correlational studies, PD participation shows a significant positive association with instructional practices (r = .20, p < .001; 95% CI [.11, .29]) but a non-significant association with student achievement (r = .06, p = .11; 95% CI [-.02, .13]). Quasi-experimental studies (N = 7 for student achievement) are summarized narratively due to limited count, showing mixed effects closer to zero. The authors caution that most primary studies are correlational (87%), with frequent shortcomings in reporting/handling sampling weights, clustering/nesting, and plausible values, so the meta-analytic results should not be interpreted as causal PD effects. data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is not an empirical ML paper and does not train or evaluate machine-learning models on ILSA microdata. It is a review/meta-analysis that aggregates effect sizes from heterogeneous primary studies, so fields such as ILSA program-cycle-grade/domain, per-country student sample sizes, PV handling, missing-data handling, and ML techniques are not defined for the review’s own analysis. The review does, however, code whether primary studies used probability weights, clustering/nesting adjustments, and plausible values, and it reports meta-analytic correlations and heterogeneity statistics (τ2 and prediction intervals) for the synthesized outcomes.
